title: Dark square, light square
hook: A checkerboard, a cylinder and its shadow. Which square sends less light?

knows: we see the colours that are there
doesNotKnow: that the brain estimates surface colour by discounting the lighting
so the same light from the screen can look like two different greys

misconception: If two squares look different, they are different on the screen.
objective: The learner can say that squares A and B send the same light (the sampler reads the same value), that the visual system judged B lighter because it discounts the shadow, and that this guess is usually right in a real scene, because light reaching the eye is lighting times reflectance.

claims.text: Squares A and B are painted with exactly the same grey on the screen (brightness 120 of 255).
claims.source: Observation on the screen; the code is the source (strategy section 5, class 3). Demo.tsx draws A, B and the connecting strip from one constant SAME = #787878 (0x78 = 120), not a theme variable, so it is identical in light and dark mode; each cell carries data-fill for checking. The sampler readout prints the value as text. Brief check: company/domains/briefs/checks/big-ideas-cycle1-check.mjs #8.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Code and pixels both checked. Demo.tsx fills A (row 1, col 0) and B (row 3, col 3) from the one constant SAME = #787878 (0x78 = 120), and B is drawn again above the shadow layer. The shadow ellipse (blur sd 5) is at least 59 px from any point of A (computed in node), so A is not darkened. Rendered pixels in the walkthrough screenshot artifacts/walkthroughs/same-grey-in-shadow/01-predict.png: A (120,120,120), B (120,120,120). The sampler readout prints SAME_VALUE = 120.

claims.text: Caption: 'After a well-known checker-shadow illusion. Our own drawing.'
claims.source: Original drawing by the builder (a 5 × 5 checkerboard and a cylinder; not traced). The illusion it follows is Adelson's checker-shadow illusion (Adelson, 1995; described in Adelson, E. H. (2000), 'Lightness perception and lightness illusions', in Gazzaniga (ed.), The New Cognitive Neurosciences, 2nd ed.; to confirm). Per the brief's W-537 re-check, the caption names no one; if Adelson 1995 is confirmed, cm-big-ideas may let it name him. Not opened by the builder.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Convention: the caption string in Demo.tsx is 'After a well-known checker-shadow illusion. Our own drawing.'; the board is a 5 x 5 grid drawn from code constants with a code-drawn cylinder, not an image. The caption names no one. Adelson 1995/2000 was not opened, so the caption must not name him until a session can open it (as the source field says).

claims.text: Your eyes judged B lighter than the light it sends: the difference came from you, not the screen. That is a guess about the world (reveal paragraphs 1-2).
claims.source: Follows from c1 and the learner's own prediction: equal light from A and B was seen as two different greys, so the difference was added by the viewer, not the screen. No cause (shadow knowledge or local contrast) is claimed. | Before the 2026-10-15 rewording: Follows from c1 and the learner's own prediction: equal light from A and B was seen as two different greys, so the difference was added by the viewer. The stage stands for the cause: 'Remove the shadow' takes away the cylinder and the shadow while A and B keep their paint. Wording change from the brief: 'lighter than the light it receives' became 'lighter than the light it sends' (the light that comes from B to the eye).
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): The support does not carry the claim. What the derivation shows: equal light from A and B (c1) seen as different greys means the difference came from the viewer. It does not show the cause given ('your visual system knows shadows darken surfaces, so...'). That is a claim from perception science, and the stage cannot isolate it: on this board B is surrounded by shadowed dark squares (69) and A by lit light squares (210), so simple local contrast predicts the same percept, and 'Remove the shadow' changes B's neighbours (69 -> 120) as well as the shadow, so it does not separate the two explanations. No openable source covers the shadow account (OpenStax Psychology 2e has no lightness-constancy passage), and adding one would put a second held sentence in the reveal next to Helmholtz (c4), against big-ideas-strategy D4. Fix (demo-builder): reword the sentence to its derivable part, e.g. 'Your eyes judged B lighter than the light it sends: the difference came from you, not the screen.' Or give it an H source and the fallback wording, and drop c4 to keep one held sentence. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): DISPUTED. STILL DISPUTED. The reveal sentence and its support ('derivation') are unchanged. The pass-38 objection is about the support and the stage, not about a missing source: the derivation shows the difference came from the viewer, but not that the visual system 'knows shadows darken surfaces'. On this board local contrast predicts the same percept (B among dark shadowed squares, A among light lit ones), and 'Remove the shadow' changes B's neighbours as well as the shadow. No allow-listed source changes that. Fix unchanged (demo-builder): 'Your eyes judged B lighter than the light it sends: the difference came from you, not the screen.' Or give it an H source (it would then be a second held sentence beside c4, which cm-big-ideas must rule on under D4). New, opened this pass: J Vis 2025 25(12): 14, 'Relationships among lightness illusions uncovered by analyses of individual differences' (PMC12517106). It says shadowed illusions, including a simplified Adelson checker-shadow, 'can be understood as variants of simultaneous lightness contrast, but the explicit shadow enhances the illusion in general'. That fits pass 38's point that local contrast and the shadow are both in play on this board. | Reset to unverified by demo-builder (2026-10-15): W-864 / FC38-41 fix applied: reveal sentence cut to its derivable part ('Your eyes judged B lighter than the light it sends: the difference came from you, not the screen'); the cause 'your visual system knows shadows darken surfaces' is gone, so local contrast vs shadow is not decided by the card. Paragraph 2 still opens 'That is a guess about the world.'

claims.text: Hermann von Helmholtz called perception 'unconscious inference'.
claims.source: Held citation, the lesson's one (class P: public domain). Helmholtz, H. von (1867), Handbuch der physiologischen Optik, vol. 3 ('unbewusster Schluss'; to confirm the section). Not opened by the builder. Cut if not checkable; fallback (brief W-537 re-check): 'Psychologists call this kind of guess an inference.' (no name; support: convention).
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): HELD (class P, the lesson's one held citation). Helmholtz 1867, Handbuch der physiologischen Optik vol. 3, could not be opened (no public-domain copy reachable; archive.org and Gutenberg blocked). Not verified on trust. Fallback per the brief: 'Psychologists call this kind of guess an inference.' OpenStax Psychology 2e 'Sensation versus Perception' (m82192) gives the nearby idea that perception includes top-down processing ('knowledge and expectancy driving a process'), but it does not use the word inference for perception, so the fallback is a convention, not a sourced fact. | FC pass 41 (fact-checker, 2026-10-15): VERIFIED. Learner text (Demo.tsx line 66): 'Hermann von Helmholtz called perception unconscious inference.' Opened on PMC: Cristalli (2022), 'Unconscious inferences in perception in early experimental psychology: From Wundt to Peirce', J Hist Behav Sci 58(4): 432-448 (PMC9796652). It says 'Helmholtz's full-blown inferentialism is contained in the third book of his Handbuch der Physiologischen Optik ... 1867'. It quotes Helmholtz 1867, p. 430: 'Die bezeichneten unbewussten Schlüsse'. It quotes Boring: 'The doctrine of unconscious inference (unbewusster Schluss) is historically a very important part of Helmholtz's theory of perception'. Helmholtz's Handbuch itself is not opened; this history-of-psychology paper is the basis. Note: c3 (same lesson) is still disputed, and the strategy question pass 38 raised (one held sentence per reveal, D4) belongs to cm-big-ideas, not to me.

claims.text: Where it stops: the light you see is lighting times how much the surface reflects, so a shadowed square sending the same light really is lighter, and in a real scene the guess is usually right.
claims.source: Light reaching the eye = illumination × reflectance. Same light L, shade illumination below sun illumination, so reflectance in shade = L / E_shade > L / E_sun (cycle-1 check script, W-537 block: 0.8 against 0.2 in illustrative units). On the stage the shadow multiplies by 4/7 (210 → 120, 120 → about 69; c6), so B's surface is the light kind. The brief moved the Adelson limit citation off the learner path; the derivation carries the limit.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Derivation: for a matte surface, light sent to the eye = illumination x reflectance. Same light L under lower illumination E_shade < E_sun needs reflectance L / E_shade > L / E_sun, so the shadowed square really is the lighter surface. On the stage the shadow multiplies by 4/7 (210 -> 120), so B is a 210-type light square: the model agrees. 'Usually right in a real scene' holds conditionally: whenever the shadow is real, judging B as lighter matches its reflectance. The recall's paper example is the same derivation.

claims.text: The board's shading (light squares 210 and dark squares 120 in the light; a shadow layer that takes light squares to 120 and dark ones to about 69) is the lesson's model, not a measurement.
claims.source: Demo.tsx constants LIGHT_LIT (210), SAME (120) and SHADOW_OPACITY (3/7: 210 × 4/7 = 120, 120 × 4/7 ≈ 69), a black layer with a blurred edge. Square B is drawn again on top of the shadow from SAME, so its value is exactly 120 by construction. Chosen so that a light square in shadow sends the same value as a dark square in the light.
claims.note: FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): Convention checked against the code: LIGHT_LIT #d2d2d2 = 210, SAME = 120, SHADOW_OPACITY 3/7, so a black layer at 3/7 gives 210 x 4/7 = 120 and 120 x 4/7 = 68.6 -> 69. Screenshot pixels in the shadow core: a shadowed dark square reads (69,69,69) and a shadowed light square (120,120,120).

recall.question: Two sheets of paper send exactly the same light to your camera. One is in shade, one is in sun. Which sheet is whiter?
recall.why: Light reaching the camera is lighting times how much the paper reflects. The shaded sheet gets less light, so to send the same amount it must reflect more: it is the whiter sheet.
